content: Tarnish is a form of corrosion that forms on metals such as copper, brass, silver, and aluminum, as well as on some semi-reactive metals, as a result of oxidation. This process is similar to rusting but occurs at a slower rate. It typically manifests as a grey or black film on the surface of the metal. To prevent tarnish on items that are primarily for display rather than regular use, a process called tinning can be employed. Tinning involves coating the reactive metal surface with a non-reactive substance, such as tin or wax, to create a protective barrier against oxygen. For items that are used more frequently, such as silverware, tarnish can be effectively prevented through regular use and cleaning with a mild dish soap. To remove tarnish, a simple and safe method involves a process similar to electrostripping, which is particularly effective for flatware and hollowware. Begin by lining a pot with aluminum foil and preparing a diluted solution consisting of equal parts baking soda, salt, and liquid soap—typically a quarter cup of each per gallon of water. Place the tarnished silver in the pot, bring the solution to a simmer, and let it sit for 10 to 20 minutes. During this time, the oxides on the silver will transfer to the aluminum, which will darken as a result. Discard the aluminum foil and thoroughly wash the silver before use. Another method for removing tarnish involves applying a drop of water and a small amount of fluoride toothpaste onto a tissue. Rub the mixture onto the tarnished silver (or other metals, though silver is most commonly affected by tarnish) to restore its shine.
